blocks.content: An LLD interview hands you a fuzzy, real world problem, "design a parking lot", "design a ride sharing app", and asks you to turn it into clean, working classes in about forty five minutes. It is less about coding speed and far more about how you think.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974110772-5095593.png

Most candidates fail not because they cannot write code, but because they have no plan. They hear the prompt, panic, and start throwing random classes on the board. Five minutes in, the interviewer is lost, and so are they.

This lesson gives you a calm, repeatable strategy that works on every LLD problem. We will walk through each step in depth, then design a full parking lot from scratch using the exact same steps. Learn this once and every LLD question starts to feel familiar.

blocks.title: How to use this lesson
blocks.content: Read it once end to end to see the whole approach. Then keep the eight step framework handy and apply it to practice problems until it becomes second nature.
1. What an LLD Interview Actually Tests
blocks.text: 1. What an LLD Interview Actually Tests

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942176019-47414030.png
blocks.alt: What an LLD interview scores you on

blocks.content: Before the how, understand the what. When an interviewer watches you design, they are quietly scoring a specific set of skills, and code correctness is only one of them.

["Can you turn a vague prompt into clear, agreed requirements?","Can you find the right classes and give each one a single clear job?","Do your classes connect through sensible relationships?","Do you apply design principles naturally, without forcing them?","Can your design absorb a new requirement without falling apart?","Do you communicate your thinking clearly the whole way through?"]
items: Can you turn a vague prompt into clear, agreed requirements?
Can you find the right classes and give each one a single clear job?
Do your classes connect through sensible relationships?
Do you apply design principles naturally, without forcing them?
Can your design absorb a new requirement without falling apart?
Do you communicate your thinking clearly the whole way through?

blocks.content: Notice that most of these are about structure and communication, not syntax. A candidate who designs a simple, clean system and explains it well beats one who writes clever code in silence.

blocks.title: The core truth
blocks.content: LLD interviews reward clear thinking over clever code. A simple design you can fully explain always beats a fancy design you cannot.
The Mindset: Think Before You Code
blocks.text: The Mindset: Think Before You Code

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942177604-187814613.png
blocks.alt: Plan first leads to clean design, rushing leads to a tangled mess

blocks.content: The single biggest mistake in LLD is rushing to code. The prompt feels like a race, so candidates start writing a class in the first thirty seconds. This almost always ends in a tangled mess.
Strong candidates do the opposite. They slow down at the start, ask questions, and sketch a plan. That upfront thinking feels slow but it makes the rest of the interview fast and smooth.
Five minutes of clarifying and planning saves twenty minutes of confused rework. Slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.

blocks.title: Two candidates, same prompt
blocks.text: Candidate A starts coding a Car class immediately and gets stuck when pricing comes up. Candidate B spends five minutes clarifying scope and listing entities, then codes calmly and finishes with time to spare. Candidate B is the hire.

blocks.content: 2. The Complete Framework
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782971895764-426194392.png
blocks.alt: The eight step LLD framework, from clarify to follow ups

blocks.content: Here is the backbone you can lean on for any LLD problem. Eight steps, in order. You will not always spend equal time on each, but you should touch them in this sequence.

["Clarify the requirements and agree on the scope.","Define the use cases and the actors who use the system.","Identify the core entities, the main nouns of the problem.","Map the relationships between those entities.","Apply design principles to keep responsibilities clean.","Choose design patterns only where they genuinely help.","Write the core classes and their key methods.","Handle the follow up questions and extensions."]
items: Clarify the requirements and agree on the scope.
Define the use cases and the actors who use the system.
Identify the core entities, the main nouns of the problem.
Map the relationships between those entities.
Apply design principles to keep responsibilities clean.
Choose design patterns only where they genuinely help.
Write the core classes and their key methods.
Handle the follow up questions and extensions.

blocks.content: The rest of this lesson takes each step in turn, explains exactly what to do, and then shows all eight working together on a real problem.
A framework turns a scary open prompt into a calm checklist. You are never lost, because you always know which step you are on.
Step One: Clarify the Requirements
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942179181-36547447.png
blocks.alt: Clarifying a vague prompt into an agreed scope

blocks.content: Never design until you know what you are building. Prompts are deliberately vague, so your first job is to pin down the scope with a few sharp questions.

["What are the core features that must work?","Who uses the system, and what do they need to do?","What is explicitly out of scope for this session?","Are there rules or limits, like pricing or capacity?"]
items: What are the core features that must work?
Who uses the system, and what do they need to do?
What is explicitly out of scope for this session?
Are there rules or limits, like pricing or capacity?

blocks.title: Clarifying a parking lot
blocks.text: Ask: does it have multiple levels? Multiple entry and exit gates? Different vehicle sizes? How is pricing decided? Agreeing these turns a vague prompt into a concrete, finishable problem.

blocks.content: Finish this step by repeating the scope back in your own words and getting a yes. Requirement Clarification has its own full lesson, because it is that important.
3. Step Two: Define the Use Cases
blocks.text: 3. Step Two: Define the Use Cases

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942180863-901564941.png
blocks.alt: Use cases become the methods of the system

blocks.content: Once you know the features, list the concrete actions the system must support. These use cases become the methods your classes will need.
For a parking lot, the use cases are simple and clear.
["A vehicle enters and is given a parking spot.","A ticket is issued at entry.","A vehicle exits and the fee is calculated.","The system tracks which spots are free."]
items: A vehicle enters and is given a parking spot.
A ticket is issued at entry.
A vehicle exits and the fee is calculated.
The system tracks which spots are free.

blocks.content: Writing the use cases early keeps your design honest. Every class you create should exist to support one of these actions.
4. Step Three: Identify the Entities
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942182397-377099819.png
blocks.alt: Turning the nouns in the requirements into entities

blocks.content: The important classes are usually the nouns in the problem. Read the requirements and underline them. Nouns become entities, verbs become methods.

blocks.title: Nouns in the parking lot
blocks.text: A vehicle enters the lot through a gate, takes a ticket, parks in a spot on a level, and pays a fee. Nouns: Vehicle, ParkingLot, Gate, Ticket, Spot, Level, Fee.

codes.python:
from enum import Enum
import time


class VehicleType(Enum):
    CAR = "CAR"
    BIKE = "BIKE"
    TRUCK = "TRUCK"


class Vehicle:
    def __init__(self, plate, vehicle_type):
        self.plate = plate
        self.type = vehicle_type


class Spot:
    def __init__(self, spot_id, fits):
        self.id = spot_id
        self.fits = fits
        self.free = True


class Ticket:
    def __init__(self, ticket_id, vehicle, spot, entry_time):
        self.id = ticket_id
        self.vehicle = vehicle
        self.spot = spot
        self.entry_time = entry_time


if __name__ == "__main__":
    car = Vehicle("KA-01-HH-1234", VehicleType.CAR)
    spot = Spot(101, VehicleType.CAR)
    ticket = Ticket("T-1", car, spot, int(time.time()))

    print(f"Vehicle plate: {ticket.vehicle.plate}")
    print(f"Vehicle type: {ticket.vehicle.type.value}")
    print(f"Assigned spot id: {ticket.spot.id}")
    print(f"Ticket id: {ticket.id}")

blocks.content: Not every noun becomes a class, but this gives you a strong first draft in seconds. Identifying Entities has its own lesson with the full technique.
5. Step Four: Map the Relationships
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942183977-899987623.png
blocks.alt: Relationships between the parking lot entities

blocks.content: Entities alone are just a pile of classes. Ask how each pair relates, using two simple questions: is a, or has a.

{"headers":["Relationship","In the parking lot"],"rows":[["Has a (composition)","A ParkingLot has Levels, a Level has Spots"],["Has a (association)","A Ticket refers to a Vehicle and a Spot"],["Is a (inheritance)","A Car is a Vehicle, a Truck is a Vehicle"]]}

class ParkingLot { List<Level> levels; }   // has a
class Level { List<Spot> spots; }          // has a
class Car extends Vehicle { }              // is a
blocks.code:
class ParkingLot { List<Level> levels; }   // has a
class Level { List<Spot> spots; }          // has a
class Car extends Vehicle { }              // is a

codes.javascript:
class ParkingLot { List<Level> levels; }   // has a
class Level { List<Spot> spots; }          // has a
class Car extends Vehicle { }              // is a

blocks.content: These relationships decide which class holds a reference to which, and turn your noun list into a real design.
6. Step Five: Apply Design Principles
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942185504-668637297.png
blocks.alt: Single Responsibility splits a god class into focused classes

blocks.content: Keep each class focused on one job. The most useful principle here is Single Responsibility: a class should have one reason to change.
For example, do not let the Spot class also calculate pricing. Pricing changes for business reasons, spots change for physical reasons. They are different jobs.

blocks.title: Do not overdo it
blocks.content: Principles have a cost. Apply them to solve a real problem, not to look advanced. A handful of clean classes beats a maze of tiny ones.
7. Step Six: Choose Patterns Wisely
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942187162-303649545.png
blocks.alt: Signals in the problem point to the right design pattern

blocks.content: Reach for a design pattern only when the problem clearly calls for one. Patterns are tools, not trophies.
{"headers":["Signal","Pattern that fits"],"rows":[["Several pricing rules","Strategy"],["Create the right vehicle by type","Factory"],["Notify displays when a spot frees up","Observer"]]}
If no pattern fits, use plain classes. Choosing Design Patterns has its own lesson on when each one earns its place.
8. Step Seven: Write the Core Classes
blocks.text: 8. Step Seven: Write the Core Classes

blocks.content: Now put it together in code. Write the key classes with their fields and the methods that support your use cases. You do not need every line, just enough to show the structure clearly.
Notice how the class reads like the use cases: park and unpark. Good structure makes the code almost describe itself.
9. Step Eight: Handle Follow Ups
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942193693-663868687.png
blocks.alt: Extend the design by adding a new class, do not rewrite

blocks.content: You are not done when the first design works. The interviewer will push: "now add electric charging spots", "now support monthly passes". A clean design absorbs these by adding classes, not rewriting them.
["Restate the new requirement in your own words.","Name what kind of change it is, a new type or a new rule.","Show where it slots into your existing design."]
items: Restate the new requirement in your own words.
Name what kind of change it is, a new type or a new rule.
Show where it slots into your existing design.

blocks.content: Handling Follow up Questions has its own lesson, because this phase often decides the result.
10. A Full Worked Example: Parking Lot
blocks.text: 10. A Full Worked Example: Parking Lot

blocks.content: Let us run the entire framework end to end, so you see how the steps connect into one smooth flow.
Clarify and scope
Assume a multi level lot, several gates, three vehicle sizes, and hourly pricing. Monthly passes are out of scope for now.
Use cases
["Park a vehicle and issue a ticket","Find a free spot that fits the vehicle","Unpark and calculate the fee"]
items: Park a vehicle and issue a ticket
Find a free spot that fits the vehicle
Unpark and calculate the fee

blocks.content: Entities and relationships
ParkingLot has Levels, a Level has Spots, a Ticket links a Vehicle to a Spot, and Car and Truck are kinds of Vehicle.
The core classes
The service that ties it together
blocks.text: The service that ties it together

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974125247-962164793.png
blocks.alt: The parking lot class diagram, the implementation structure

blocks.title: The follow up
blocks.text: Interviewer: add different pricing for weekends. Answer: pricing is already a Strategy, so I add one WeekendPricing class and inject it. No existing class changes. That is the whole design paying off.

blocks.content: Every step flowed into the next, and the final follow up was easy because the earlier steps kept the design clean. That is the power of the framework.
11. Managing Your Forty Five Minutes
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942190518-587296288.png
blocks.alt: How to budget the forty five minutes of an LLD interview

blocks.content: Time is a resource you must budget. Here is a sensible split for a typical session.

{"headers":["Phase","Rough time","Goal"],"rows":[["Clarify and use cases","8 minutes","Agree scope and actions"],["Entities and relationships","10 minutes","A clear class map"],["Core class design","15 minutes","Clean classes with methods"],["Follow ups and extensions","10 minutes","Show the design can grow"]]}

blocks.title: The classic time trap
blocks.content: Do not spend twenty minutes on a perfect diagram and then run out of time to write classes. Keep every phase moving.
12. Communicate While You Design
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782942192083-68635231.png
blocks.alt: Narrating your thinking is a strong signal, silence is weak

blocks.content: A silent designer is a scary designer. Narrate your thinking so the interviewer can follow, agree, and even nudge you back on track.

["Say what step you are on: \"let me clarify the scope first\".","Explain each choice: \"I will make pricing its own class so it can change independently\".","Check in: \"does this scope sound right before I design?\".","Think out loud when stuck, so the interviewer can help."]
items: Say what step you are on: "let me clarify the scope first".
Explain each choice: "I will make pricing its own class so it can change independently".
Check in: "does this scope sound right before I design?".
Think out loud when stuck, so the interviewer can help.

blocks.content: The interviewer cannot read your mind. Every good decision you make in silence is a decision they did not see you make.
13. What Interviewers Are Scoring
Behind the friendly chat, the interviewer is filling a mental scorecard. Knowing it helps you aim.

{"headers":["They check","How you show it"],"rows":[["Requirement handling","You clarify before designing"],["Class design","Each class has one clear job"],["Extensibility","New features add classes, not edits"],["Communication","You explain your thinking clearly"]]}
Aim to give clear evidence for each row, and you will score well even if the design is not perfect.
14. Common Mistakes

{"pros":["Clarify before designing","Talk through your thinking","Start simple, then extend","Give each class one job","Use patterns only when they help"],"cons":["Coding in the first minute","Designing in silence","Chasing a perfect first pass","One giant class doing everything","Forcing patterns to look clever"]}
15. Common Questions
Should I start with UML or code? - Either works. Clarify and list entities first, then use whichever helps you think. The UML First vs Code First lesson compares them.
What if I cannot think of a pattern? - Then do not use one. Clean plain classes are always acceptable. Patterns are a bonus, never a requirement.
How much code should I actually write? - Enough to show the structure: the key classes, fields, and important methods. You rarely need every line.
What if I get stuck halfway? - Return to the requirements and entities. Almost every stuck moment is fixed by re grounding in what the system must do.
Is it fine to change my design midway? - Yes. Say why you are changing it. Adapting cleanly is a strength, not a weakness.
16. Key Takeaways

["LLD tests clear thinking and communication, not just code.","Never code before you clarify and plan.","Follow the eight steps: clarify, use cases, entities, relationships, principles, patterns, code, follow ups.","Keep each class focused on a single responsibility.","Use patterns only when the problem genuinely calls for them.","A clean design absorbs follow ups by adding classes, not rewriting.","Talk out loud the entire time."]
items: LLD tests clear thinking and communication, not just code.
Never code before you clarify and plan.
Follow the eight steps: clarify, use cases, entities, relationships, principles, patterns, code, follow ups.
Keep each class focused on a single responsibility.
Use patterns only when the problem genuinely calls for them.
A clean design absorbs follow ups by adding classes, not rewriting.
Talk out loud the entire time.

blocks.content: Master this framework and LLD stops being scary. Every problem becomes the same calm sequence, and the lessons that follow drill deep into each step.
